props.title: How to Steal a Million
props.initialSlug: Audrey Hepburn plots to steal fake art she owns

sections.content: How to Steal a Million (1966) sparkles as one of the most sophisticated heist comedies ever made, pairing Audrey Hepburn and Peter O'Toole at their most charismatic. Like Charade (1963) and To Catch a Thief (1955), it masterfully blends romance with elaborate art crime, but adds a delicious twist - Hepburn's character must steal back her family's forged artwork before it's exposed. Director William Wyler, who previously directed Hepburn in Roman Holiday (1953), brings his signature polish while letting the stars' chemistry drive the story. movies.title: How to Steal a Million
movies.slug: Audrey Hepburn and Peter O'Toole team up to steal a fake statue from a museum to protect her art forger father's reputation

sections.content: The film sits perfectly within the 1960s trend of stylish European-set capers like Topkapi (1964) and The Pink Panther (1963). But while those lean harder into farce, Wyler maintains sophisticated wit throughout. The museum heist sequence is a masterclass in building tension through comedy, as Hepburn and O'Toole hide in a cramped closet and execute an ingenious plan involving a boomerang and precise timing. The film's Parisian locations and Givenchy costumes create an atmosphere of effortless elegance that later influenced films like The Thomas Crown Affair (1968).

Beyond its surface charms, the film cleverly subverts expectations about art crime. Unlike The Train (1964) or Monuments Men (2014), which treat art theft as serious cultural robbery, How to Steal a Million plays with ideas of authenticity and value. The fact that Hepburn must steal a fake piece that her family created raises amusing questions about art world pretensions. This theme would later be explored more dramatically in films like F for Fake (1973) and Exit Through the Gift Shop (2010). movies.slug: A sophisticated gang plans an elaborate heist of a Turkish museum's prized dagger

sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later romantic heist movies that balance comedy with genuine tension. Hudson Hawk (1991) directly references its museum heist techniques, while Ocean's 8 (2018) echoes its focus on art world schemes and glamorous settings. The dynamic between Hepburn and O'Toole - initially antagonistic but growing into romantic complicity - became a template for films like The Hot Rock (1972) and the remake of The Thomas Crown Affair (1999).
